The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has said six attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz were reported in the past week, while shipping traffic remained about 65 percent below pre-war levels.

In its weekly report published on Friday, UKMTO said four of the six incidents occurred in the Strait of Hormuz and two in the Arabian Gulf. 

The UKMTO recorded 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits during the seven days to November 18, including US-facilitated movements. The combined figure was down from 139 outbound and 169 inbound the previous week.

Around half of Strait of Hormuz transits involved energy carriers. Most vessels broadcasting AIS continued to use the Iranian route, although UKMTO noted an increase in traffic along the southern route.

No attacks were recorded in the past week in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandab, with the last confirmed attack recorded on August 24. However, vessel transits through Bab el-Mandeb remain about 22 percent below levels existing before 22 July when Houthis announced a blockade.

Josh Gruenbaum, who was appointed to the council by Trump and previously worked in the White House, told Ynet: “We have been extremely patient and have given Israel its space. “If this political leadership says it no longer wants to honour what they committed to, just let us know,” Gruenbaum said “And we will throw the keys back to the UN.”

Ynet said it had seen a presentation prepared by council members, who visited Israel last week. Its final slide, titled “Other alternatives to Gaza”, reportedly lists several scenarios if the plan is abandoned.

These include a future US administration and Congress ordering a different reconstruction plan, the UN Security Council taking over “perhaps through UNRWA”, the Palestinian Authority and Hamas.

The last scenario, according to the slide, is that Israel becomes fully responsible for the administrative and humanitarian costs of Gaza’s population.

Another slide reportedly says Hamas formally accepted the plan in July, pledging to give up its weapons and transfer governmental powers to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the technocratic body meant to run the territory.

“We are at a standstill due to political elements within the Netanyahu government who have prevented us from progressing and from testing whether Hamas will keep its word,” Gruenbaum said, according to Ynet.

In a working paper submitted at the review session for the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, the group said the current treaty has glaring gaps that allow for the use of white phosphorus.

Lana Nusseibeh's bid to become the next secretary-general of the United Nations suffered a setback on Friday after the UK, France and China all voted against the Emirati diplomat in the latest informal straw poll conducted to help determine who should replace Antonio Guterres.

Along with the US and Russia, the countries make up three of the P5, the permanent members of the UN Security Council that can veto any prospective candidate for the world body's top job.

The US, Russia and Israel - which is not currently part of the Security Council and thus does not vote - all back Nusseibeh, according to the same sources.

In total, the UAE minister of state and former ambassador to the UN received seven "encourage" votes, six "discourage" votes and two "no opinion" votes - the same result she achieved in the last straw poll, held on 6 November.

Candidates need to secure at least nine votes to then be put forward to the UN General Assembly, but in order for this to happen they need to have no "discourage" votes.

The frontrunner, the Costa Rican economist and diplomat Rebeca Grynspan, has 10 encourage votes, but two discourage votes from members of the P5, believed to be Russia and the US.

Argentina's Rafael Grossi, who is backed by his country's far-right president Javier Milei and is favoured - like Nusseibeh - by the US, also picked up three discourage votes from members of the P5.

With no agreement among the P5, the process remains deadlocked. 

Nusseibeh has vowed to stay in the race, posting on X: "I remain fully committed to this campaign and will continue engaging Member States to earn their support and make the case for a more active, results-focused and responsive United Nations."

Lobbying from the UAE

The results remain a setback for the Abu Dhabi-born diplomat, who has been relentless in her pursuit of the job despite fierce opposition from civil society focused mainly on her country's involvement in the war in Sudan.

In her official role in the UAE's government, Nusseibeh has denied reports from the UN Panel of Experts on Abu Dhabi's sponsorship of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force found to have committed genocide in Darfur by the UN and the US.

On Friday, MEE reported on efforts she had made to lobby Iain Duncan Smith, after the former leader of the UK's Conservative Party spoke out in parliament about the UAE's “sponsoring of a huge amount of terrorism in Sudan” and called on the British government to use its Security Council veto to block her nomination.

Exclusive: UAE's Nusseibeh lobbied UK's Iain Duncan Smith over UN candidacy

The former government minister told MEE that in his meeting with Nusseibeh he reiterated the position he had taken in parliament about the UAE’s involvement in Sudan - denied by Abu Dhabi - and called for the release of “two British citizens wrongly held in Dubai: Ryan Cornelius and Charles Ridley”.

Duncan Smith told Nusseibeh that the UAE needed to “cease and desist” from its involvement in the Sudan war.

He told Nusseibeh that her UN candidacy gave the UAE a chance to do the right thing and withdraw from the war in Sudan and release Cornelius and Ridley, two British citizens who have been detained in Dubai for almost 20 years.

“They are corrupt, and they are corrupting,” Duncan Smith said of the Emiratis, before calling on UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to "take a stand".

It would appear that this stand has been taken by Britain, as well as France and China. Nusseibeh and the UAE remain committed to her candidacy, though, and can use what one former British government official described to MEE as "money and investment" as leverage.

Responding to MEE's request for comment on Friday, a spokesperson for Nusseibeh’s campaign said: “Lana Nusseibeh is meeting a wide range of stakeholders as part of her candidacy for UN secretary-general.

"We do not comment on the content of private meetings. Lana has taken a leave of absence from her ministerial role since the submission of her nomination. She took this decision as part of her genuine commitment to the independence of her campaign and potential future role.”

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Explosive-laden boxes dropped from the sky: Israel’s latest weapon in Gaza
item.description:
Explosive-laden boxes dropped from the sky: Israel’s latest weapon in Gaza

Submitted by Abdallah al-Naami on Fri, 11/20/2026 - 12:08
Palestinian families recount how Israeli quadcopters drop explosives on to their homes, demolishing entire buildings and displacing dozens of families
Jaber Yaseen stands amid the rubble of his home, destroyed by explosive-laden boxes dropped by an Israeli drone in Gaza City’s al-Zaytoon neighbourhood (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
Off

Jaber Yaseen's family was preparing the traditional maftoul dish for their Friday family lunch when they heard a loud engine approaching.

The Palestinian family of 13 were startled by the noise, which grew louder as it approached their home in al-Zaytoon neighbourhood, east of Gaza City.

“I thought it was an Israeli tank at first. I looked out of the window and was shocked to see a huge quadcopter drone carrying two boxes of explosives, flying low over our neighbourhood,” Yaseen told Middle East Eye.

“I watched the drone move towards us. Without any warning, it dropped the two boxes of explosives on to our roof. I was terrified for my children's lives. I grabbed them and rushed out of the house, knowing the explosives could detonate at any moment. We couldn't take anything with us.”

Panic spread as families watched more Israeli drones dropping explosives on to rooftops across the neighbourhood. Dozens were forced to flee their homes, with nowhere to go.

A group of residents gathered at a distance, watching as the quadcopter drones continued to drop explosives. Minutes later, the devices on the rooftops began detonating.

For 33-year-old Ismail Madi, watching the drones was heartbreaking.

“We had been displaced several times before, and each time I held on to some hope that we would return home. But when I saw the quadcopter drones carrying explosives above our home, I felt as though I had left my soul behind as I walked away,” Madi told MEE.

Abdaljawad Badwan, another resident of the neighbourhood, described the terror of watching the attack unfold.

“Everyone was shocked and terrified. Every time an explosion went off, we hoped it would be the last. But the drones kept coming back with more boxes.”

Families told MEE that the initial explosions were intended to create openings in the roofs.

Large quadcopter drones, measuring approximately 4m across, then continued to drop nearly 60 boxes of explosives inside each house.

The explosives were subsequently detonated, destroying the houses and damaging many surrounding buildings.

By 10pm (8pm GMT), the Israeli attack on 13 November had completely demolished three multi-storey houses and severely damaged dozens of others.

Nearly 33 families lost their homes that night.

Forced into the streets

With their homes destroyed, Palestinian families were left without shelter in the cold night.

“We had nowhere to go for shelter. All 13 of us spent the night on the pavement. We are still living on the pavement in a makeshift tent that I built the following day,” Yaseen said.

The sudden displacement has compounded the suffering these families were already enduring.

“We spent the night on the street, surrounded by piles of rubbish, rodents and insects. My two-year-old son, Abdalsamad, was very sick, and I had to go around asking neighbours for painkillers late at night,” said Badwan, a father of four.

'I built this home brick by brick. I don't know how to describe what I feel'

- Jaber Yaseen, Gaza resident 

In the early hours of the morning, families returned to inspect their homes. They were confronted with scenes of devastation.

“I have lived here my entire life, yet I could barely recognise my neighbourhood because of the sheer scale of destruction,” Madi said.

For him, the aftermath was particularly devastating. He had married just two months earlier.

“I put a lifetime of hard work into preparing my home and saving for my wedding. I had hoped to begin a new chapter of my life there, with a sense of stability and safety. I was overwhelmed with grief when I saw my home and everything I had worked for destroyed before my eyes,” Madi told MEE.

Standing amid the rubble of his home, Yaseen struggled to put his feelings into words.

“I built this home brick by brick. I don't know how to describe what I feel. It's heartbreaking. I find myself crying every night just thinking about my home,” he told MEE.

‘We face death every day’

Since returning to their neighbourhood following the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, families in al-Zaytoon have faced a daily struggle for survival.

Being located near the so-called "Yellow Line" - a military boundary imposed by Israeli forces inside the Gaza Strip - has meant a consistent threat from Israeli soldiers nearby. 

“We face death every day,” Madi told MEE.

“The Yellow Line is just 50m away. Israeli quadcopter drones and tanks come every day and open fire towards our homes. These attacks have become part of our daily routine. We have no choice but to adapt. We have even taught the children how to hide when the shooting starts.” 

Israel’s expanding ‘Yellow Line’ swallows Gaza districts and uproots families
Read More »

Israeli forces have steadily pushed the "Yellow Line" westwards over the past year, encroaching on residential areas, often without warning.

“We have lived in constant danger for the past year. We could wake up any day to find that the [Israeli] army has moved the yellow blocks westwards, past our homes, and that we have to evacuate,” Yaseen said.

The daily attacks are not the only hardship these families face. Living in an area classified as dangerous by humanitarian aid organisations, they receive little to no assistance.

Families say that the nearest source of water, medical centre or school is 2km away. Adults and children must make the dangerous journey every day, despite the recurring Israeli attacks.

“We have adapted to the daily Israeli attacks and the lack of aid because we wanted to stay in our homes. The quadcopter attack was shocking. I never imagined something like this could happen, especially without any warning,” Yaseen said.

A new tactic to displace families? 

Despite the so-called ceasefire in Gaza, Israel has continued its attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,600 Palestinians, destroying homes and expanding its control through military force.

Last week's attack on al-Zaytoon neighbourhood marked a new development, with Israeli forces using quadcopter drones to plant boxes of explosives inside homes in a populated area outside the "Yellow Line". Families had barely enough time to escape before watching their homes being destroyed.

The attack was not an isolated incident.

'I was born and raised in this home. I cannot live away from it'

- Ismail Madi, Gaza resident 

Over the past week, Israel has escalated its use of quadcopter drones carrying boxes of explosives, destroying Palestinian homes and property outside the "Yellow Line" in al-Maghazi, al-Musadder, Khan Younis and al-Nuseirat.

As these attacks grow in intensity and frequency, families across Gaza fear that explosive-laden quadcopter drones are becoming a central part of Israel's tactics to destroy what remains of Palestinian homes in Gaza and forcibly displace residents.

“We are worried that Friday's attack was a message or a threat from the [Israeli] army telling us to leave the area, and that perhaps we won't be allowed to return to it in the near future,” Yaseen told MEE.

On Thursday, for the first time since the so-called ceasefire, Israel announced the launch of a ground attack outside the "Yellow Line" in al-Nuseirat, in central Gaza.

During the preceding night, Israeli forces destroyed several buildings in northern al-Nuseirat using boxes of explosives planted by quadcopter drones.

But despite the destruction of their homes and the catastrophic conditions they face, families were quick to return to al-Zaytoon neighbourhood after the attack. 

“I spend the day here in the neighbourhood. My soul is attached to my home, even though it is now just a pile of rubble,” Yaseen told MEE.

“I'll build my tent here, next to the remains of my home. I'd rather die than live away from home.” 

For Madi, returning to the neighbourhood is about more than his attachment to his home.

“I was born and raised in this home. I cannot live away from it,” he told MEE.

“By staying here in the neighbourhood, we are the first line of defence for the community. Our steadfastness gives other families living near the Yellow Line a sense of hope and safety.”
